node.conditionals.title: Making the program choose (a grade classifier)

steps.prompt: True or False?
steps.body:
Before the computer can choose, it has to ASK a question it can answer with
just True or False. You ask with a COMPARISON:

    number = 1
    number == 1   ->  True
    number == 2   ->  False
    number != 2   ->  True
    number > 0    ->  True

Note the DOUBLE equals `==`. One `=` stores a value (`number = 1`); two `==`
*compares* two values and hands back True or False. They are different tools.
steps.carryContext: `==` compares (gives True/False); a single `=` stores a value. `!=` is "not equal".

Which line asks that correctly?

back True or False), not the one that stores a value.

Write `is_one(n)` that returns the string "match" when n equals 1, and

cells.title: Running one block or the other

steps.prompt: if / else
steps.body:
Now hand that True/False question to an `if`. The computer runs the indented
block ONLY when the question is True; otherwise it runs the `else` block.

    number = 1
    if number == 1:
        print("Your number is 1")
    else:
        print("Your number is not 1")

Two things are non-negotiable:
  * the COLON `:` at the end of the `if` / `else` line, and
  * the INDENTATION of the block that belongs to it.
Exactly ONE of the two blocks runs — never both, never neither.
steps.carryContext:
`if condition:` then an indented block; optional `else:` block. Exactly one block runs.
Header line ends in a colon.

if / elif / else
steps.body:
Two answers is not enough when a score can earn many grades — A, B, C, or F.
Chain conditions with `elif` ("else if"):

    if score >= 90:
        print("A")
    elif score >= 80:
        print("B")
    elif score >= 70:
        print("C")
    else:
        print("F")

The computer checks TOP-DOWN: first the `if`, then each `elif` in order. The
FIRST condition that is True wins — its block runs and the rest are skipped.
`else` is the catch-all fallback when nothing above matched.

Because 95 is `>= 90` AND `>= 80` AND `>= 70`, ORDER matters: test the highest
cutoff first so a top score lands on "A", not on a broader branch below. Each
`elif` line is a comparison too, so it uses an operator like `>=`, never a single `=`.
steps.carryContext:
`if` then `elif ...:` branches then optional `else:`. Checked top-down, first True wins,
rest skipped. `else` is the fallback. Test the highest / most-specific cutoff FIRST.

steps.prompt:
score is 95. Both `>= 80` and `>= 90` are True — but only ONE branch runs.
Which line prints? (Remember: top-down, first True wins.)

One of these `elif` lines crashes with a SyntaxError. Which line is
WRITTEN CORRECTLY?

Build the grade classifier. Write `grade(score)` that returns exactly ONE
letter, using if / elif / else with comparisons:
  score 90 or above  -> "A"
  score 80 to 89     -> "B"
  score 70 to 79     -> "C"
  anything below 70  -> "F"
Remember: the checks run TOP-DOWN and the FIRST true one wins, so test the
highest cutoff first.
The computer wants to talk back

steps.prompt: The computer can repeat itself
steps.body:
Last time you built a guessing game where the human guesses once and the computer
says **too low**, **too high**, or **just right**. One guess is tedious — nobody
nails 1–100 on the first try.

A `while` loop repeats an indented block **as long as a condition stays True**:

```python
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print("snacks!")
    count = count - 1
```

The header ends in a colon; the indented body runs, then Python re-checks the
condition at the top. When `count > 0` is finally False, the loop stops and the
program moves on.
steps.carryContext:
A `while` loop = a header `while <condition>:` plus an indented body. The body runs
over and over while the condition is True; Python re-checks the condition at the top
of every pass.

steps.prompt: `n` starts at 3. How many lines does this print, and what are they?
steps.code:

while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
print("done")

steps.prompt: Loop the guess, not just the message
steps.body:
Here is the one-shot game again — the computer picks a secret 1–100 and judges a
single guess:

```python
import random
number = random.randint(1, 100)
guess = int(input())
if number == guess:
    print("correct")
elif number > guess:
    print("too low")
else:
    print("too high")
```

To let the human keep guessing, we wrap the read-and-judge in a loop. The tempting
move is `while True:` — "just keep going":

```python
while True:
    guess = int(input())
    if number > guess:
        print("too low")
    elif number < guess:
        print("too high")
```

But `while True` never stops on its own — its condition is *always* True. A loop
needs a way **out**: either a `break` when the guess is right, or a condition that
eventually turns False.
steps.carryContext:
A loop must TERMINATE. `while True:` is an infinite loop unless something inside it
runs `break`. The alternative is a condition that becomes False — e.g.
`while guess != number:` — but only if the body actually updates `guess`.

choices.label: The body reads `guess = int(input())` each pass — when guess equals number the condition is False and the loop ends.

node.output.title: Let's make the computer talk to us

cells.title: Tell the computer to say something

steps.prompt: Text lives inside quotes
steps.body:
We're going to make the computer talk. But first: how do we hand it
words?

We wrap the words in **quotes**:

    "Hello World!!! I'm ALIVE and I demand snacks!!"

That whole thing — quote to quote — is a **string**. Every character
between the quotes counts: the letters, the spaces, the exclamation
marks, even the apostrophe in "I'm". Spaces, dashes, and symbols are
all just characters. The quotes are the fence that says "this is text,
treat it literally, don't try to run it."
steps.carryContext:
A string is text inside quotes; spaces/dashes/symbols all count as
characters. The quotes mark it as literal text.

steps.prompt: print(...) puts it on the screen
steps.body:
Now we make it talk. The command is `print`, and we hand it our
string inside the parentheses:

    print("Hello World!!! I'm ALIVE and I demand snacks!!")

Run that and the computer says:

    Hello World!!! I'm ALIVE and I demand snacks!!

Two pieces, both required: the **call** — the word `print` followed by
`( )` — and the **string** sitting inside the parentheses.
steps.carryContext:
print("...") = the call `print(...)` wrapped around a string literal.
Both the call and the quotes are required.

steps.prompt: What is an RNG?
steps.body:
Ever wonder how a video game decides where the next enemy spawns, or whether
you land a critical hit? A **random number generator** (RNG). Python ships one
in the `random` toolbox.

Two steps, always:

1. Open the toolbox: `import random`
2. Ask for a number in a range: `random.randint(1, 100)`

`random.randint(a, b)` hands you a whole number somewhere from `a` to `b` —
and both ends are **included**. So `random.randint(1, 100)` can give you `1`,
it can give you `100`, or anything in between.
steps.carryContext:
To use random numbers you must FIRST `import random`, then call
`random.randint(a, b)`. The range is inclusive of BOTH a and b.

steps.prompt: The + that glues text
steps.body:
You already know a string is text in quotes. Here is the trick: the same `+`
you'd use on numbers also **ties strings together** end to end.

    print("This " + "is" + " cool!")

Run that and the computer prints:  `This is cool!`

The computer is greedy — it does NOT sprinkle in spaces for you. Every space you
want in the output has to live **inside the quotes**. Look closely: that's `"This "`
with a space tucked in before the closing quote, and `" cool!"` with a space right
after the opening quote. Leave them out and the words slam together.
steps.carryContext:
Joining text: `"a" + "b"` makes `"ab"`. Spaces only appear if they are INSIDE the
quotes. The + lives OUTSIDE the quotes — it is the glue, not a character.

steps.prompt: Write greet(name) so it returns a greeting like  Hi Alan!  — the word "Hi", then a space, then the name, then an exclamation mark. Glue the pieces with +.
Text and numbers don't speak the same language
steps.body:
Gluing text to text works great. But the moment you try to glue a piece of text
onto a **number**, the computer throws up its hands.

Python refuses to guess what you meant — it will NOT quietly turn a number into
text for you. You have to ask, in one of two ways:

    str(number)            # turn the number INTO text, then glue:  "n: " + str(7)
    f"...{number}..."       # an f-string drops the number straight in:  f"n: {7}"

Both print  `n: 7`. Pick whichever you like.
steps.carryContext:
`"text" + number` is an ERROR (TypeError) — Python won't auto-convert. Fix it with
`str(number)` or an f-string `f"...{number}..."`. Both turn the number into text first.

steps.prompt: A variable is a labelled box
steps.body:
A **variable** is a storage box with a name on the front. You do two things:
first you pick a name for the box (let's literally call it `name`), then you put
something in with the equals sign — the box's name on the **left**, the value on
the **right**:

    name = "Alan"

The value here is a string, so it needs quotes (you met quotes in the last node).
`name` now holds the text `Alan`. The box keeps it until you put something else in.
steps.carryContext:
Assignment goes name = value: NAME on the LEFT, VALUE on the RIGHT.
A string value needs quotes: name = "Alan".

steps.prompt: We forgot the quotes. What does Python do?
You want to store the text `Alan` in a box called `name`. Which line does that?

cells.title: Reusing what is in the box

steps.prompt: Open the box by writing its name (no quotes)
steps.body:
To **use** what's in a box, you write the box's name with **no quotes** — that hands
Python the value inside. You can copy one box into another, then print it:

    name = "Alan"
    anotherName = name        # copy the value across
    print(anotherName)        # -> Alan

Because the box holds a string, you can join strings onto it with `+`. Mind the
space — it lives INSIDE the quotes, before the closing quote:

    print("My name is " + name)   # -> My name is Alan

Quotes are the difference: `name` (no quotes) means "the value in the box";
`"name"` (quotes) means the literal four-letter word.
steps.carryContext:
Unquoted name = the VALUE in the box. Quoted "name" = the literal word.
Join text with + ; keep the trailing space inside the quotes: "My name is " + name.

skill.bool.compare.title: Compare two values to get True/False
skill.bool.compare.description: Compare values with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>` to get True or False.

misconceptions.title: Uses a single `=` (assignment) where `==` (comparison) is meant
misconceptions.feedback:
`=` and `==` are different tools. A single `=` STORES a value (`number = 1`). To
ASK whether two values are equal you need DOUBLE equals `==`, which gives back True
or False. Writing `if number = 1:` is a SyntaxError — Python refuses to run it.

hintLadder.body: You want to ask a question, not store a value. Is one `=` enough?
One `=` assigns. Comparing for equality needs a different, doubled operator.
To check equality use `==`: `if number == 1:` gives True or False.
Solution:
hintLadder.revealCode: number == 1

misconceptions.title: Uses `is` for value equality instead of `==`
misconceptions.feedback:
`is` asks "are these the exact same object in memory?", which is NOT the same as
"do these have the same value". For small ints it sometimes *looks* right, but it
is the wrong tool and fails in general. To compare VALUES for equality, use `==`.

hintLadder.body: `is` and `==` ask different questions. Which one is about VALUE?
`is` is identity (same object). You want equality of value.
Use `==` for value equality: `number == 1`.
Solution:
hintLadder.revealCode: number == 1

skill.cond.if_else.title: Run one of two blocks with if/else
skill.cond.if_else.description: Run exactly one of two blocks (colon + indentation; branches are mutually exclusive).

misconceptions.title: Forgets the `:` ending the if/elif/else header
misconceptions.feedback:
Every `if`, `elif`, and `else` HEADER line must end with a colon `:`. The colon is
what tells Python "an indented block belongs to me." Leaving it off (or using `;`)
is a SyntaxError. `if number == 1:` — note the trailing colon.

hintLadder.body: What punctuation marks the end of an `if` header, before the indented block?
It is not `;`. Python uses a colon to open a block.
End the header with `:` — `if number == 1:` — then indent the block.
Solution:
hintLadder.revealCode: if number == 1:

misconceptions.title: Believes both the if-block and the else-block run
misconceptions.feedback:
Only ONE block runs. If the condition is True, the `if` block runs and the `else`
block is SKIPPED entirely; if it is False, only the `else` block runs. Never both.
The two blocks are mutually exclusive — exactly one fires every time.

hintLadder.body: If the `if` condition is True, does Python still bother with the `else`?
`else` means 'otherwise'. It only runs when the `if` was False.
Exactly one block runs: the `if` block OR the `else` block, never both.
With number == 1 True, only this prints:
hintLadder.revealCode: Your number is 1

skill.cond.elif_chain.title: Chain conditions with elif
skill.cond.elif_chain.description: Chain conditions with `elif`; checked top-down, first true wins, `else` is the fallback.

misconceptions.title: Uses `=` (assignment) inside an `elif` condition
misconceptions.feedback:
An `elif` condition is a COMPARISON, so it needs an operator like `>=` or `==`,
not a single `=`. `elif score = 80:` tries to ASSIGN inside the condition, which
Python rejects as a SyntaxError. Write `elif score >= 80:`.

hintLadder.body: An `elif` asks a question. Is a single `=` a question or a command?
Just like `if`, an `elif` condition compares — it needs `>=` / `==`, not `=`.
Fix the assignment to a comparison: `elif score >= 80:`.
Solution:
hintLadder.revealCode: elif score >= 80:

misconceptions.title: Orders overlapping conditions so an earlier branch shadows a later one
misconceptions.feedback:
The computer checks branches TOP-DOWN and the FIRST True one wins — the rest are
skipped. A condition that is too broad (or placed too early) will swallow values
meant for a later branch, so that later branch never runs. With `>=` cutoffs, test
the HIGHEST cutoff first: `>= 90`, then `>= 80`, then `>= 70`, then `else`.

hintLadder.body: A 95 should be an "A", but you returned "C". Which branch caught it first?
An earlier, too-broad condition fires first and skips the rest. Check branch ORDER and breadth.
Test the highest cutoff first: `if score >= 90:` / `elif score >= 80:` / `elif score >= 70:` / `else:`.

mis.concat.plus_in_quotes.feedback: The `+` ended up INSIDE the quotes, so the computer treated it as a plus-sign character to print rather than as glue. A `+` between two quoted pieces does the joining; a `+` inside quotes is just text. Move the plus outside the quotes.

hintLadder.body: Is the + you typed inside the quotes or outside them?
A `+` inside quotes is a literal character. The joining `+` must sit OUTSIDE the quotes, between two strings.
You wrote something like `"Hi " + "+" + name`, which prints a stray +. You only need the pieces of the message joined: `"Hi " + name + "!"`.

mis.concat.str_num.title: Glued text directly to a number — expected Python to auto-convert
mis.concat.str_num.feedback: That's the big one! `"text" + number` crashes with a TypeError — Python will not secretly turn a number into text. You have to convert it yourself: wrap the number in `str(...)`, as in `"Your random number is: " + str(number)`, or use an f-string: `f"Your random number is: {number}"`. Both turn the number into text first.

hintLadder.body: Read the error. What two kinds of things did you try to glue together with +?
Text and numbers are different types. `+` can join text-to-text, but not text-to-number. You must convert the number to text first.
Two ways to convert: `"...: " + str(number)` turns the number into text, or an f-string `f"...: {number}"` drops it straight in.
Solution:

mis.var.assign_reversed.title: Writes the assignment backwards: value on the left
mis.var.assign_reversed.feedback:
`"Alan" = name` reads right-to-left in your head, but Python needs the BOX on the left
and the VALUE on the right: `name = "Alan"`. You can't put a label on a value — only a
value into a box. (Python even says "cannot assign to literal".)

hintLadder.body: Which side of the `=` gets the name of the box, and which side gets the value?
The box name is always on the LEFT of `=`; the value goes on the RIGHT. You wrote them swapped.
To store the text Alan in a box called name, the box comes first: `name = "Alan"`.
Solution:

used the name before its `name = ...` line ran, or you wrote a value without quotes
(`name = Alan`) so Python looked for a box called `Alan` that doesn't exist. Assign the
box first; quote text values.

hintLadder.body: Python says a name 'is not defined'. Was that box ever filled with a `=` line before you used it?
A name with no quotes makes Python look for ANOTHER box by that name. If you meant the text, it needs quotes.
Assign before you use, and quote text: `name = "Alan"` THEN `print(name)`.

mis.var.use_quoted.title: Quotes the variable name, printing the word instead of the value
mis.var.use_quoted.feedback:
Wrapping the box name in quotes — `"name"` — turns it into the literal four-letter word,
so the greeting always says "My name is name". Drop the quotes to hand Python the VALUE
inside the box: `"My name is " + name`. Quotes = literal text; no quotes = the variable.

Quotes make text literal. `"name"` is the word; `name` (no quotes) is the value in the box.
